interface.name: inox_window_manager_v1
interface.description:
Private, unstable Inox protocol that lets the desktop's own shell observe and drive window management.
Why this is a protocol and not a link. The compositor owns windows, their placement, focus and the workspaces they live on; the panel draws them as task buttons. `AGENTS.md` §2 forbids a Cargo dependency between the two, so the panel cannot ask the compositor's data structures directly. What it needs is narrower than the compositor's whole state: *which windows exist, what they are called, which workspace and output they are on, and which one has the focus*, plus four verbs — activate, minimize, close and set mode — and the workspace switches that go with a task bar. None of that is in `xdg-shell` (a client may not ask about another client's toplevel), and `inox-ipc` is a session-wide control global bound once per connection rather than a per-observer subscription. Hence a global of its own.
What this protocol is not. It grants no window content, no pixels and no screen reading: the events carry handles, strings and enumerations, and the requests are the same actions a user already has through a keyboard binding. Binding it does not make a client the window manager — the compositor keeps every decision, and a request it cannot or will not honour is answered by `request_failed`, never by a silent no-op the caller could mistake for success.
Who may bind it. Every client may, exactly like `inox_ipc`: what a client learns here (titles and application ids) is what the task bar shows on screen anyway, and the requests are ordinary user-level window actions. A future revision that adds a privileged verb must add the authorization with it rather than widening this one.
Versioning. `inox-window-manager-v1` follows `inox-ipc`'s rules: it is unstable until Inox 1.0, it may change incompatibly, and consumers negotiate through the version the global is bound at instead of assuming a revision.

request.name: get_window_list

description.summary: observe and drive the managed windows

request.description:
Create an observer of the compositor's managed windows. The new `inox_window_list_v1` immediately receives `session_generation`, then `workspace_state`, then one `window` event per managed window in the compositor's layout order, and finally `snapshot_done`. Everything after that is incremental.
A client may create more than one list object, and each one is served independently: a client that drops a list and creates another gets a fresh snapshot, which is how a reconnect rebuilds its view without having to track what it missed.

interface.name: inox_window_list_v1

description.summary: one observer's view of the managed windows

interface.description:
The events of this object are the compositor's authoritative statement about its windows, and the panel treats them as such: a window's state here is what it draws, not what it asked for.
Handles. `window` is assigned by the compositor and is opaque to the client: it is not a process id, not a title and not a position in the list, all of which can be reused for a different window. A handle is only meaningful together with the `session_generation` it was issued under, which is why the generation is sent before any handle: a client that reconnects to a restarted compositor must not match an old handle against a new window.
Read-back, not acknowledgement. A request here does not get a success event, because a compositor that said "done" before the change reached the screen would be lying: the `window` event carrying the new state (or `window_removed` for `close`) *is* the confirmation, and a client shows the effect it reads back rather than the request it sent. Failures are the exception and are reported, because a silent no-op would let a task button stay disabled for ever with nothing to log.

enum.name: window_mode

description.summary: how the compositor is showing a window

enum.description:
A window is in exactly one of these modes. They are not independent flags: maximizing a tiled window replaces tiling, and returning to `tiled` restores the window to the tiling layout. `minimized` is separate and orthogonal — a window keeps its mode while it is away.
The mode is the compositor's statement about what it is doing, and a client that asked for something else learns the truth from the next `window` event rather than from the request it sent.

entry.name: floating
entry.summary: placed freely, outside the tiling layout

entry.name: fullscreen
entry.summary: filling the whole output, above the shell surfaces

description.summary: why the compositor did not carry out a request

entry.name: unknown_window
entry.summary: no window with that handle is managed any more

entry.name: not_permitted
entry.summary: the session's policy refuses this change

request.name: activate

description.summary: bring a window to the front and give it the keyboard

request.description:
Switch to the workspace the window is on, leave `minimized` if it is there, and make it the focused window. This is what a task button does when the user clicks a window that is not already focused.
If the session is locked, the request fails with `not_permitted`: no ordinary window may be focused behind a lock.

request.name: minimize

description.summary: put a window away, keeping it managed

request.description: The window stops being composited and loses the focus, but keeps its handle, its mode and its workspace, so activating it later restores it where it was. This is what a task button does when the user clicks the window that already had the focus.

request.name: close
request.description: Sends `xdg_toplevel.close` to the client. This is a request to the application, not a kill: it may save first, prompt, or refuse, and the compositor keeps managing the window until the client destroys the toplevel. The confirmation is therefore `window_removed`.

request.name: set_mode

description.summary: change how a window is shown

request.description: Ask the compositor to show `window` in `mode`. The compositor applies the placement the mode implies — `maximized` fills the output's work area, so an exclusive-zone panel stays uncovered, while `fullscreen` fills the whole output — and reports the result with a `window` event.

request.name: move_to_workspace

description.summary: move a window to another workspace

request.description:
Move `window` to `workspace`, which must be a workspace number below the count reported by `workspace_state`; anything else fails with `not_permitted` rather than creating a workspace nothing can reach.
A window moved to the workspace the user is looking at stays focused; a window moved away leaves the focus to the next window of the workspace it left.

arg.name: workspace
arg.summary: the zero-based workspace to move it to

request.name: switch_workspace
request.description:
Make `workspace` the active one. Every window on it is composited again and the windows of the workspace being left stop being composited; each affected window is announced with a `window` event when its `visible` flag changes, so a client's view stays exact without having to re-snapshot.
Out-of-range numbers fail with `not_permitted`, like `move_to_workspace`.

event.name: session_generation

description.summary: the session the handles below belong to

event.description:
Sent once, before any handle. Handles from another generation are stale and must be discarded rather than compared numerically with the ones that follow: a compositor restart re-uses small integers for different windows.
The value is advisory. A Wayland connection cannot outlive the compositor that served it, so this exists to let a client keep the ordering of its own view honest, not to authenticate anything.

arg.name: generation
arg.summary: the generation this session's handles belong to

event.name: workspace_state

description.summary: how many workspaces there are and which one is shown

event.description: Sent when the list is created and again whenever either number changes. `active` is zero-based and always below `count`; `count` is at least one, because a desktop with no workspace has nowhere to put a window.

event.name: window
event.description:
Sent once per managed window while the snapshot is built, and again whenever anything about it changes: its title or application id, its mode, whether it is minimized, whether it is visible on the active workspace, whether it has the focus, or where it lives. It carries the complete state rather than a delta so that a client which missed an event still converges on the next one.
`output` is the connector the window is on, as the compositor spells it ("eDP-1", "headless-1"), or the empty string while no display is available and the window is managed but unplaced.
A window is announced only once it has drawn something: a toplevel that exists but has no buffer takes no tile and gets no task button, and announcing it would put a button on screen for a window that may never appear.

arg.name: app_id
arg.summary: the application id the client set, possibly empty

arg.name: title
arg.summary: the title the client set, possibly empty

arg.name: workspace
arg.summary: the zero-based workspace the window is on

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the connector name, or empty when unplaced

arg.name: mode
arg.summary: how the window is being shown

arg.name: minimized
arg.summary: 1 while the window is put away, else 0

arg.name: visible
arg.summary: 1 while the window is on the shown workspace and not minimized, else 0

arg.name: focused
arg.summary: 1 on the window that has the keyboard, else 0

event.name: window_removed
event.description: The window's toplevel was destroyed, so the handle is dead: it is never re-issued, and a request naming it fails with `unknown_window`. This is also how a `close` request is confirmed to have been carried out.

event.name: snapshot_done
event.description: Sent after the last `window` of the snapshot, so a client can tell an empty desktop from a snapshot it has not finished receiving. Nothing else is sent until it has.

event.name: request_failed

description.summary: a request was not carried out

event.description:
Sent instead of the state change the request asked for. A client must not treat a request as done because it was sent: the confirmation is the `window` or `window_removed` event, and this is the other outcome.
`window` is the handle the failed request named, so a client holding one request per window can match the failure to the request it has in flight.

arg.name: window
arg.summary: the window the failed request named
